definitionSection.title: What is a Derivative?
definitionSection.subtitle: Core Mechanics & Fundamental Purpose
definitionSection.description: A Derivative is a financial contract whose value is derived from—and dependent on—the performance of an underlying asset, benchmark, or index.

purposeSection.title: Strategic Purpose
purposeSection.subtitle: Four Core Drivers of the Derivative Market
purposeSection.description: Derivatives are not merely speculative tools; they are essential instruments that allow market participants to insulate operations from volatility, allocate capital efficiently, and establish accurate global price signals across interconnected markets.

list.title: Risk Hedging
list.description: Protects portfolios and business operations against adverse price movements, currency fluctuations, or interest rate spikes by locking in prices or setting downside floors.

list.title: Price Discovery
list.description: Reflects global market expectations and real-time news into future asset valuations, serving as an early indicator of supply, demand, and spot market trends.

list.title: Leverage & Capital Efficiency
list.description: Enables market participants to control large positional exposure with a relatively small upfront capital requirement (margin or premium).

list.title: Speculation & Arbitrage
list.description: Allows investors to generate returns from anticipated market direction, while traders exploit temporary price discrepancies across different markets or instruments.

productSection.title: Core Derivatives Products
productSection.subtitle: Building Blocks of Risk Management
productSection.description: The global derivatives landscape is anchored by four primary contract structures—each engineered to handle specific risk profiles, settlement mechanisms, and operational preferences ranging from standardized exchange environments to tailored bilateral agreements.

list.title: Futures
list.description: Standardized, exchange-traded agreements to buy or sell an asset at a predetermined price on a specified future date, marked-to-market daily.

list.title: Forwards
list.description: Private, customizable Over-The-Counter (OTC) agreements between two parties to exchange an asset at a fixed price on a future date.

list.title: Options
list.description: Contracts that give the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy (Call) or sell (Put) an asset at a specified strike price within a set timeframe.

list.title: Swaps
list.description: Agreements between two counterparties to exchange sequences of cash flows over a period, typically based on interest rates, currencies, or commodities.

overview.title: Futures Contracts
overview.subtitle: Standardized, Exchange-Traded Agreements
overview.description: Futures contracts are standardized agreements to buy or sell a specific asset at a set price on a future date. Traded on centralized exchanges, they are marked-to-market daily to minimize default risk.

howItWorks.title: How It Works
howItWorks.description: Futures operate within strict regulatory frameworks and standardized contract specifications, ensuring liquidity and removing direct counterparty negotiations.

list.title: Standardized Agreement
list.description: Two parties enter into a legally binding contract on a centralized exchange to buy or sell a specific asset at a predetermined price on a specified future date. The exchange standardizes the contract size, quality grade, and expiration date so it can be easily traded.

list.title: Margin & Leverage (Collateral Deposit)
list.description: Instead of paying the full value of the asset upfront, both the buyer and seller deposit a fraction of the total contract value—known as the initial margin—into a brokerage account as collateral to guarantee performance.

list.title: Daily Mark-to-Market (MTM)
list.description: At the end of every trading day, the exchange revalues the contract based on current market prices. Any profits or losses are credited or debited directly to the trader's margin account daily. If losses dip below a required threshold, a margin call is triggered, requiring immediate cash top-ups.

list.title: Offset or Settlement
list.description: Before the contract expires, most market participants close out their position by taking an opposite trade to lock in profits or losses. If held until expiration, the contract is settled either via physical delivery of the underlying asset or through cash settlement, depending on the contract type.

features.title: Product Mechanics
features.subtitle: Standardized Contracts & Daily Settlement
features.description: Futures operate within strict regulatory frameworks and standardized contract specifications, ensuring liquidity and removing direct counterparty negotiations.

list.title: Exchange Standardization
list.description: Fixed contract sizes, expiration dates, and quality specifications defined by the exchange (e.g., CME).

list.title: Daily Mark-to-Market (MTM)
list.description: Gains and losses are settled daily into trader margin accounts, preventing cumulative credit risk.

list.title: Margin Requirements
list.description: Requires Initial Margin (to enter) and Maintenance Margin (to hold), enforcing financial collateral.

list.title: Central Clearinghouse
list.description: Acts as the buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer, virtually eliminating counterparty credit risk.

benefits.title: Primary Drivers & Benefits
benefits.subtitle: Liquidity, Leverage, and Price Certainty
benefits.description: Market participants rely on futures to lock in forward pricing and gain capital-efficient exposure across major global asset classes.

list.title: Operational Hedging
list.description: Producers and consumers (e.g., airlines, farmers) lock in future input/output prices to stabilize margins.

list.title: High Liquidity
list.description: Deep order books allow institutional investors to enter and exit large positions quickly with low slippage.

list.title: Capital Efficiency
list.description: High leverage capabilities allow traders to control large exposure with minimal upfront equity.

list.title: Transparent Pricing
list.description: Continuous open market price discovery ensures real-time valuation and tight bid-ask spreads.

risks.title: Risk Factors & Limitations
risks.subtitle: Managing Leverage and Rigidity
risks.description: While highly liquid, futures carry rigid commitments and leverage dynamics that require active capital management.

list.title: Margin Call Risk
list.description: Daily price swings can trigger mandatory cash top-ups, forcing position liquidation if unfulfilled.

list.title: Obligation Risk
list.description: Parties are bound to execute at expiration regardless of how favorable or unfavorable spot market prices become.

list.title: Lack of Customization
list.description: Standardized contract sizes and dates may not perfectly align with specific operational needs.

list.title: Basis Risk
list.description: Potential mismatch between the futures price and the actual cash spot price of the underlying asset upon hedge settlement.

overview.title: Forward Contracts
overview.subtitle: Bespoke Over-The-Counter (OTC) Agreements
overview.description: Forwards are private, non-standardized bilateral contracts to buy or sell an asset at a set price on a future date. Tailored directly between two parties, they offer complete operational flexibility.

howItWorks.title: How It Works
howItWorks.description: Unlike futures, forwards are built directly between counterparty institutions without exchange intervention or daily cash rebalancing.

list.title: Bilateral Over-the-Counter (OTC) Customization
list.description: Two parties (typically a corporate client and a bank or another corporation) negotiate a private agreement directly with one another, off-exchange. They customize every single term of the contract—including the exact asset, precise volume or notional amount, delivery location, and specific maturity date—to match their exact operational needs.

list.title: No Upfront Premium or Margin Required
list.description: Unlike futures or options, entering into a forward contract generally requires zero upfront cost or margin deposit. The agreed-upon price (the forward price) is locked in at inception, reflecting the current spot price adjusted for storage costs, convenience yields, and the time value of money (interest rate differentials).

list.title: Interim Non-Settlement (No Daily Mark-to-Market)
list.description: Throughout the contract's lifespan, market prices for the underlying asset will fluctuate. However, unlike exchange-traded futures, there are no daily cash adjustments, margin calls, or intermediate settlements. The contract remains active and static on the balance sheets of both parties until maturity, meaning unrealized gains or losses accumulate quietly in the background.

list.title: Terminal Settlement at Expiry
list.description: At the predetermined maturity date, the contract is fulfilled according to its terms. Depending on how it was structured, this final settlement is executed either via physical delivery (the buyer pays the locked price and takes delivery of the physical commodity or currency) or cash settlement (the net financial difference between the spot price at expiry and the locked forward price is paid in cash between the parties).

features.title: Product Mechanics
features.subtitle: Bilateral Customization & Single Settlement
features.description: Unlike futures, forwards are built directly between counterparty institutions without exchange intervention or daily cash rebalancing.

list.title: Bilateral OTC Structure
list.description: Negotiated directly between two institutions (typically corporation and bank) off-exchange.

list.title: 100% Customizable Terms
list.description: Asset size, exact delivery date, grade, and delivery location are tailored to precise specifications.

list.title: Single Point Settlement
list.description: Cash or physical settlement occurs exclusively at contract maturity—no daily mark-to-market.

list.title: Private Contracts
list.description: Terms, pricing, and counterparty identities remain private and unlisted from public market exchanges.

benefits.title: Primary Drivers & Benefits
benefits.subtitle: Precision Matching and Cash Flow Certainty
benefits.description: Corporations utilize forward contracts when standardized exchange contracts fail to match their exact timeline, volume, or currency specifications.

list.title: Perfect Hedge Alignment
list.description: Eliminates basis risk by matching contract size and delivery date exactly to corporate cash flows.

list.title: No Daily Cash Drag
list.description: Absence of daily margin calls avoids intermediate cash flow disruptions during the contract lifecycle.

list.title: Tailored Foreign Exchange (FX) Protection
list.description: Widely used by importers and exporters to lock in exact future exchange rates.

list.title: Flexible Settlement Modes
list.description: Designed for either actual physical delivery of goods or net cash settlement at expiry.

risks.title: Risk Factors & Limitations
risks.subtitle: Counterparty Vulnerability and Illiquidity
risks.description: The primary trade-off for customization in forward contracts is credit exposure and the inability to exit early.

list.title: Counterparty Credit Risk
list.description: High risk of default if the opposing party fails to perform at maturity, as no clearinghouse guarantees the trade.

list.title: Illiquidity & Lock-In
list.description: Secondary markets do not exist; unwinding or transferring a forward before maturity requires bilateral consent.

list.title: Zero Price Transparency
list.description: Lack of public pricing quotes makes fair value estimation dependent on internal modeling.

list.title: Unrealized Loss Accumulation
list.description: Settlement at maturity means losses accumulate over the term rather than being paid down daily.

overview.title: Options Contracts
overview.subtitle: Asymmetric Rights and Tailored Payoffs
overview.description: Options provide the buyer the right—but not the obligation—to buy (Call) or sell (Put) an asset at a fixed strike price. This creates asymmetric risk profiles with capped downside and open upside potential.

howItWorks.title: How It Works
howItWorks.description: Option dynamics depend on two distinct roles: option buyers who purchase flexibility, and option writers who absorb risk for a premium.

list.title: Purchasing the Right (Not the Obligation)
list.description: A buyer enters into a contract by paying a non-refundable upfront fee called the premium to an option writer (seller). In exchange, the buyer acquires the right—but not the obligation—to either buy (Call Option) or sell (Put Option) an underlying asset at a predetermined price (Strike Price) within a specific timeframe.

list.title: Leverage and Asymmetric Payoffs
list.description: Because the buyer controls the right to trade the underlying asset without owning it directly, they achieve high capital efficiency. The buyer's risk is strictly capped at the upfront premium paid, while their potential profit upside can be substantial (for Calls) or protected against sharp market drops (for Puts).

list.title: Time Decay and Market Valuation Dynamics
list.description: Throughout its lifespan, the option's price fluctuates based on changing market conditions—including the underlying asset's price, proximity to expiration, and market volatility. Crucially, Theta (time decay) works continuously against the option buyer, meaning the contract loses value every day as it approaches expiration if the underlying asset hasn't moved favorably.

list.title: Expiration, Exercise, or Closing
list.description: Before or at expiration, the holder has three choices: Exercise the option to buy or sell the underlying asset at the strike price, close the position by trading the option in the open market to lock in gains or cut losses, and let it expire resulting in the loss of 100% of the initial premium.

features.title: Product Mechanics
features.subtitle: Strikes, Premiums, and Asymmetric Obligations
features.description: Option dynamics depend on two distinct roles: option buyers who purchase flexibility, and option writers who absorb risk for a premium.

list.title: Calls vs. Puts
list.description: Calls confer the right to buy; Puts confer the right to sell the underlying asset.

list.title: Upfront Premium
list.description: The non-refundable cost paid by the buyer to the seller (writer) for holding the contract rights.

list.title: Strike Price & Expiration
list.description: Fixed transaction price guaranteed up to a defined expiration date.

list.title: Exercise Styles
list.description: American options can be exercised anytime before expiry; European options only on the expiration date itself.

benefits.title: Primary Drivers & Benefits
benefits.subtitle: Portfolio Protection and Non-Linear Return Profiles
benefits.description: Options are unique because they allow market participants to protect against downside risks while leaving the door open for upside gains.

list.title: Downside Insurance
list.description: Protective Puts act as an insurance policy for stock portfolios against market crashes.

list.title: Capped Risk for Buyers
list.description: Maximum loss for option buyers is strictly limited to the upfront premium paid.

list.title: Strategic Versatility
list.description: Enables income generation (Covered Calls), directional bets, or volatility trades (Straddles).

list.title: Capital Leverage
list.description: Controls significant underlying assets with relatively low capital deployment via options premiums.

risks.title: Risk Factors & Limitations
risks.subtitle: Time Decay and Unlimited Loss Potential for Sellers
risks.description: Options involve complex pricing factors, where time decay works continuously against buyers, and writers face severe risk exposure.

list.title: Theta / Time Decay
list.description: Option value naturally erodes every day as the contract approaches its expiration date.

list.title: Premium Loss Risk
list.description: A high percentage of out-of-the-money options expire completely worthless, forfeiting 100% of invested capital.

list.title: Unlimited Risk for Sellers
list.description: Naked option writers take on extreme, potentially unlimited risk for a finite upfront premium.

list.title: Pricing Complexity
list.description: Valuations depend on interconnected variables including spot price, strike, time, interest rates, and implied volatility.

overview.title: Swap Contracts
overview.subtitle: Bilateral Cash Flow Exchanges
overview.description: Swaps are customized OTC agreements between two parties to exchange sequences of cash flows over a specified timeline, typically converting floating rates or volatile exposure into fixed, predictable liabilities.

howItWorks.title: How It Works
howItWorks.description: Swaps do not involve exchanging initial principal amounts; instead, net interest or asset return differentials are calculated against a benchmark.

list.title: Bilateral Agreement on Notional Principal
list.description: Two counterparties (usually corporations, banks, or financial institutions) negotiate a private over-the-counter (OTC) agreement to exchange financial streams over a set period. They establish a notional principal amount—which is a theoretical reference figure used solely to calculate cash flows and is never actually exchanged between the parties.

list.title: Defining the Cash Flow Legs
list.description: The contract is structured around two distinct payment streams (legs) running in opposite directions. Typically, one party pays a fixed rate (providing budget certainty), while the other party pays a floating or variable rate (such as SOFR or EURIBOR) or an alternative asset's return.

list.title: Periodic Calculation & Netting Settlements
list.description: Throughout the life of the swap (often spanning years), the parties calculate their respective payment obligations at regular intervals (e.g., quarterly or semi-annually). To maximize efficiency, they use a netting mechanism: rather than sending separate payments back and forth, only the net financial difference is transferred between the parties on each settlement date.

list.title: Termination, Maturity, or Early Unwinding
list.description: The swap continues until its predetermined maturity date, at which point the final cash flow is settled and the agreement expires. If either party wishes to exit early before maturity, they cannot simply sell it on an exchange; instead, they must negotiate an offsetting swap, execute an early termination agreement, or pay a breakage fee to the counterparty.

features.title: Product Mechanics
features.subtitle: Notional Principal and Differential Cash Settlement
features.description: Swaps do not involve exchanging initial principal amounts; instead, net interest or asset return differentials are calculated against a benchmark.

list.title: Notional Principal Amount
list.description: Theoretical base amount used exclusively to calculate cash flow calculations—never actually exchanged.

list.title: Fixed vs. Floating Streams
list.description: One leg pays a fixed agreed rate, while the opposing leg pays a reference rate (e.g., SOFR, EURIBOR).

list.title: Netting Mechanism
list.description: Cash flows occurring on the same date are netted, with only the net difference transferring between parties.

list.title: Multi-Year Durations
list.description: Typically long-dated instruments ranging from 2 to 30+ years in maturity.

benefits.title: Primary Drivers & Benefits
benefits.subtitle: Balance Sheet Optimization and Debt Restructuring
benefits.description: Corporations and financial institutions leverage swaps to transform liability structures without refinancing underlying loans.

list.title: Interest Rate Risk Transformation
list.description: Converts floating-rate corporate debt into fixed-rate debt to lock in interest costs.

list.title: Currency Risk Alignment
list.description: Cross-currency swaps hedge multi-national foreign debt and matching revenue streams.

list.title: Lower Borrowing Costs
list.description: Allows counterparties to exploit relative comparative advantages in different credit markets.

list.title: Off-Balance-Sheet Flexibility
list.description: Adjusts interest rate exposure without altering or renegotiating underlying debt obligations.

risks.title: Risk Factors & Limitations
risks.subtitle: Long-Horizon Credit Exposure and Interest Rate Shifts
risks.description: Due to their extended tenors, swaps create long-term counterparty dependencies and exposure to broader structural economic shifts.

list.title: Extended Counterparty Credit Risk
list.description: Long contract durations increase the probability of counterparty default over economic cycles.

list.title: Early Termination Friction
list.description: Exiting a swap before maturity requires costly negotiation, breaking fees, or offsetting trades.

list.title: Interest Rate Direction Risk
list.description: If market interest rates move favorably opposite to your fixed lock, you incur significant opportunity loss.

list.title: ISDA Regulatory Complexity
list.description: Requires comprehensive master documentation (ISDA Master Agreements) and collateral management framework (CSAs).
